job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Issues in S. 2817 (as amended Oct. 6, 2026)

These are issues in how the bill is written, not a view on whether it should pass. Before publishing any of them, have a legal source confirm the ones you plan to report (Senate Legislative Counsel, CRS, or an ocean-law scholar).

## Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A): tonnage threshold.** Operations recovering 10,000 metric tons or less per year fall outside the prohibition entirely. "Per year" is also undefined (calendar year, fiscal year, or any rolling 12 months), which creates timing games and makes it hard to tell when a violation occurs.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "by a single vessel."** An operator could split recovery across several vessels, each staying under 10,000 tons. There is no aggregation rule by operator, project, or site.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A): recovery not done by a vessel.** The definition covers only recovery "by a vessel." Recovery from fixed platforms, seabed crawlers, or riser systems that don't fit that description may fall outside it.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "recovery" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether recovery means collecting on the seabed, lifting to the surface, or bringing onboard. An operator could collect material and stockpile it on the seabed, or lift it in a later year, to manage its annual tonnage.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "other mineral resources" undefined.** This could be read narrowly (hard minerals only) or broadly enough to reach sand, gravel, or even oil and gas. That invites both evasion arguments and overbreadth challenges.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "at depths greater than 200 meters."** The bill doesn't say whether this means water depth, depth below the seabed surface, or depth of the deposit. It also doesn't say how depth is measured (tide datum, at which point of the operation).

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B): "the Secretary" is never defined.** No department is named, though Commerce or NOAA, Interior, and State all have plausible roles. Sec. 6 separately names the Secretary of State.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B): open-ended delegation.** The Secretary can extend the prohibition to any activity posing "comparable" risks. There is no required rulemaking, notice and comment, or standard for "comparable." That exposes the clause to nondelegation and arbitrary-and-capricious challenges.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) combined with Sec. 5(b): criminal vagueness.** Criminal liability could rest on an agency determination with no defined criteria or required public notice. That creates fair-notice and vagueness problems, and courts may read the clause narrowly or decline to enforce it criminally.

10. **Sec. 2(2): narrow "U.S. person."** The definition reaches only citizens and "corporations." That arguably leaves out LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and lawful permanent residents, which matters because LLCs are a common structure for project companies.

11. **Sec. 2(2): "organized under the laws of a State."** "State" is undefined, so entities organized in DC, Puerto Rico, or other territories may be excluded.

12. **Sec. 2(2): foreign subsidiaries.** A U.S. company can operate through a foreign-incorporated subsidiary, which isn't a "U.S. person." The bill has no ownership or control test.

13. **Sec. 2(3) vs. Sec. 2(1)(A): mismatched thresholds.** The registry covers only vessels over 5,000 gross tons, but the prohibition turns on tonnage recovered. Smaller vessels could mine without registering or reporting.

## Prohibition (Sec. 3)

14. **Sec. 3(a): "in the United States" undefined.** The bill doesn't say whether the prohibition covers the territorial sea, the Exclusive Economic Zone, the outer continental shelf, or the territories. A foreign company using a foreign-flagged vessel in the U.S. EEZ may not be "in the United States."

15. **Sec. 3(a): only direct conduct is covered.** Nothing addresses financing, chartering, sponsoring, contracting for, or aiding mining. Nothing restricts importing, buying, or processing seabed-mined minerals, so U.S. companies can still fund or buy from foreign operators.

16. **Sec. 3(b): "exploration license" isn't limited to U.S. licenses.** It could be read to cover licenses or contracts from foreign states or the International Seabed Authority. That would grandfather a large share of active projects worldwide.

17. **Sec. 3(b): exploration vs. commercial recovery.** The exemption covers "mining conducted under an exploration license," yet exploration licenses generally don't authorize commercial recovery. A court could read this as allowing full commercial mining by anyone holding a pre-enactment exploration license.

18. **Sec. 3(b): no limits on grandfathered licenses.** There is no limit on renewal, extension, modification, expansion, or transfer, so a pre-enactment license could be sold or stretched indefinitely. The cutoff at enactment also creates an incentive to rush applications while the bill is pending.

19. **Sec. 3(c): "environmental assessment" exemption.** The term is undefined, has no tonnage cap, requires no permit or agency approval, and depends on the actor's stated "purpose." Commercial-scale "test mining" could be labeled assessment.

## Registry (Sec. 4)

20. **Sec. 4: no penalties.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing inaccurate reports carries no specific penalty. 18 U.S.C. § 1001 might reach false statements, but that is untested here.

21. **Sec. 4: no deadlines or content requirements.** There is no registration deadline. Reports needn't include tonnage, location, depth, or methods, which are exactly the facts needed to enforce the 10,000-ton and 200-meter thresholds.

22. **Sec. 4(b): reporting tied to registration.** Only "registered operator[s]" must report, so an operator that never registers also never reports.

23. **Sec. 4: no jurisdictional scope.** The bill doesn't say whether the registry applies to foreign-flagged vessels, vessels outside U.S. waters, or only U.S. persons. Reports are self-certified with no verification, inspection, or vessel-tracking requirement.

24. **Sec. 4: NOAA gets no rulemaking or inspection authority.** The registry is assigned to NOAA, but NOAA gets no authority to write rules or inspect. That may also conflict with whatever "Secretary" Sec. 2(1)(B) means.

## Penalties (Sec. 5)

25. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8: conflicting dates.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. That raises the question of whether conduct in the 180-day window is penalized. If it is, it may face a retroactivity or fair-notice challenge.

26. **Sec. 5(a): annual threshold vs. daily penalty.** Mining becomes a violation only after 10,000 tons in a year, but penalties accrue "for each day" of violation. The bill doesn't say whether violation starts on the day the threshold is crossed or covers every day of the year's operations.

27. **Sec. 5: no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to assess penalties. There is no administrative or judicial procedure, no injunctive relief, no vessel seizure or forfeiture, and no citizen-suit provision. There is a maximum ($1M per day) but no minimum.

28. **Sec. 5(b): "willfully."** This generally requires proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful. Combined with the ambiguous definitions above, criminal cases would be hard to bring.

## International Agreement (Sec. 6)

29. **Sec. 6: "shall seek to negotiate."** This imposes no obligation to conclude anything. "Not later than 18 months" is ambiguous: it could mean begin negotiating or finish. There is also no reporting requirement, no consequence for failure, and no definition of "equivalent." The U.S. relationship to UNCLOS and the International Seabed Authority isn't addressed.

## Duration (Sec. 7)

30. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b): direct conflict.** Subsection (a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress acts, while (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. The bill doesn't say which controls.

31. **Sec. 7(a): no NASEM study is actually required.** The bill neither commissions nor funds the report. "Serious harm" is undefined. A joint resolution needs the President's signature, so in practice it is just a new law, and the clause adds little.

32. **Sec. 7(b): no savings clause.** Without one, defendants may argue that pending enforcement actions and unpaid penalties lapse at sunset. The general savings statute (1 U.S.C. § 109) may not clearly apply to an expiration as opposed to a repeal. The sunset would also end the registry.

## Effective Date (Sec. 8)

33. **Sec. 8: 180-day window.** Mining is lawful for 180 days after enactment, which may encourage ramping up operations. Meanwhile, the grandfather cutoff (Sec. 3(b)), the negotiation deadline (Sec. 6), and the sunset (Sec. 7(b)) all run from enactment, which adds to the timing confusion.

## Cross-Cutting

34. **No conforming amendments.** The bill doesn't amend or reconcile the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.), under which NOAA issues exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits. It also doesn't address the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, under which Interior can lease OCS minerals. Agencies could keep processing applications under those laws, and companies could argue the statutes conflict.

35. **No rulemaking authority or severability clause.** Without general rulemaking authority, gaps can't be filled administratively. Without a severability clause, litigants may argue that if the broad Sec. 2(1)(B) delegation falls, related provisions fall with it, though courts generally presume severability.

## Most Consequential for Coverage

If you need to prioritize, these are likely to matter most:
- **Item 16** (foreign and ISA exploration licenses possibly grandfathered)
- **Item 17** (exploration license may permit commercial recovery)
- **Items 2 and 12** (vessel-splitting and foreign subsidiaries)
- **Item 14** (EEZ coverage unclear)
- **Item 30** (Sec. 7 internal conflict)
- **Item 34** (no reconciliation with existing licensing law)

These are also good questions to put to committee staff before or at Thursday's markup.
